![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/a51d0d8ef1be2e7fc06aa34fe1440e77a79d8bee654703c1e931332390741c32.png)

A $13\,\text{ft}$ ladder leans against the side of a building, forming an angle $\theta $ with the ground. Given that the foot of the ladder $F$ is being pulled away from the building at the rate of $0.5\,\text{ft/s}$, at what rate is $\theta $ decreasing at the moment when the top of the ladder $T$ is $12\,\text{ft}$ above the ground?
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/7b923b76e90d665a722643684ce94fff50500a7be8b70aa821410a7969e4bb79.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance from the foot of the ladder to the wall of the building, $y$ is the vertical distance between the top of the ladder and the ground, and $z$ is the length of the ladder. The quantity $z=13$ feet does not change with time because the ladder's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $y=12$ feet. To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{13} \\ x & =13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.5.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}0.5 & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{1}{26} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{26}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{12}{13} \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  & =\frac{13}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{26}\cdot \frac{13}{12}=-\frac{1}{24}.
$$

So, the angle $\theta $ is *decreasing* at a rate of $\frac{1}{24}$ radians per second.
